intro: Use these learning checklists, then try a short practice exercise when ready. Checked topics are your own assessment. Ask your recruiter which design or ML rounds apply to your role.

tracks.title: Low-level design
tracks.description: Turn requirements into classes, interfaces, state and tests.

items.title: Give each class one clear responsibility
items.explanation: Learn which data and actions belong together. Example: an account stores its balance and handles deposits; a notification sender sends messages.

items.title: Choose how objects work together
items.explanation: Learn composition versus inheritance. Explain when one object should use another object, and when two objects truly share a parent type.

items.title: Define inputs, outputs and allowed behavior
items.explanation: For each operation, name its inputs, return value and errors. Example: what does cache.get return when the key is missing?

items.title: Replace a dependency without changing callers
items.explanation: Learn why a small interface helps testing. Explain how a fake message sender or fake clock can replace the real one.

items.title: List valid states and transitions
items.explanation: Example: a job can be pending, running, completed or failed. Explain which changes are allowed and what cancellation does.

items.title: State what must always remain true
items.explanation: An invariant is a rule that every operation must preserve. Example: a cache must never exceed its capacity; a balance must obey the account rules.

items.title: Handle invalid input and missing data
items.explanation: Decide what happens for empty input, an unknown ID or an invalid value. Explain whether the caller gets an error, a default value or an empty result.

items.title: Separate temporary failures from permanent ones
items.explanation: A timeout may succeed on retry; an invalid request will not. Explain retry limits and how to avoid repeating a side effect such as charging twice.

items.title: Choose normal, boundary and failure cases
items.explanation: For a cache: test a hit, a miss, an update, zero capacity and eviction. Explain the expected result before writing a test.

items.title: Test behavior with controlled dependencies
items.explanation: Use fake clocks, storage and network responses to make tests repeatable. Check public behavior rather than private implementation details.

tracks.title: System design
tracks.description: Connect APIs, storage and services, then explain scaling and failure trade-offs.

items.title: Define users and the main workflow
items.explanation: Say who uses the system, what they need to do, and what is outside the first version. Trace one successful request before adding components.

items.title: Set traffic, latency and availability targets
items.explanation: Estimate requests per second and data size. Explain how quickly the user needs a response and how much downtime the product can tolerate.

items.title: Design requests, responses and error behavior
items.explanation: Name the main endpoints, required fields, IDs and status codes. Explain how the client checks the status of work that finishes later.

items.title: Handle repeated requests and authorization
items.explanation: Learn idempotency: repeating a request should not repeat an unwanted side effect. Explain who may call each API and how duplicate requests are recognized.

items.title: Define records and the queries they must support
items.explanation: Choose key fields, IDs and relationships. List the reads and writes the product needs before choosing a database or index.

items.title: Choose storage and consistency for a reason
items.explanation: Learn when relational tables, key-value storage and object storage fit. Explain what users see when replicas or cached data are briefly out of date.

items.title: Find the first bottleneck with a rough estimate
items.explanation: Estimate compute, storage and network demand. Explain which component reaches its limit first instead of adding every scaling technique at once.

items.title: Choose caching, queues or partitioning
items.explanation: Learn what each technique solves. Caches reduce repeated reads, queues absorb bursts, and partitions split data or work. Explain the new problems each choice creates.

items.title: Plan timeouts, retries and failure recovery
items.explanation: Trace a failed dependency or crashed worker. Explain retry limits, duplicate protection and what happens to work that repeatedly fails.

items.title: Monitor the system and recover lost data
items.explanation: Choose useful metrics and alerts. Explain backups, restore testing and how users or operators discover that processing is stuck.

items.title: Compare two reasonable designs
items.explanation: State what you gain and lose: latency versus cost, fresh data versus availability, or a simple service versus many services. Tie the choice to the requirements.

items.title: Explain how the first version can evolve
items.explanation: Keep the initial design small. Identify one signal that would justify a bigger design, and explain how you would change it without losing data.

reading.section: Chapter 3: requirements, APIs and data modelling
reading.goal: Trace one request and identify which component owns each piece of data.
Choose a cache, queue, timeout or fallback only when it solves a stated problem.

tracks.title: ML / GenAI design
tracks.description: Design useful AI behavior with evaluation, access control and recovery.

items.title: Explain the path from documents to retrieved evidence
items.explanation: Learn parsing, chunks, embeddings, indexes and ranking. Trace one question from search to the pieces of evidence used in the answer.

items.title: Keep retrieved evidence useful and authorized
items.explanation: Learn keyword versus vector search, permission filters and document freshness. Explain how the system avoids using documents the user cannot access.

items.title: Define tool contracts and action permissions
items.explanation: Say which tools the assistant can call, what each accepts and returns, and which actions need approval. Treat instructions inside retrieved content as untrusted data.

items.title: Bound the workflow and preserve its state
items.explanation: Set limits on steps, time and cost. Explain how the assistant stops, resumes interrupted work and avoids performing the same external action twice.

items.title: Build a small test set with expected outcomes
items.explanation: Include normal questions, missing evidence, conflicting documents and access restrictions. Define a good answer and a harmful failure before choosing a model.

items.title: Measure retrieval and answer quality separately
items.explanation: Check whether search found the right evidence, then whether the answer used it correctly. Track unsupported claims, task success, latency and cost.

items.title: Respond clearly when evidence is weak or missing
items.explanation: Explain when to ask a clarifying question, show partial evidence or say the answer is unknown. Do not invent facts to fill a gap.

items.title: Recover from model and tool failures safely
items.explanation: Plan timeouts, bounded retries and useful fallback behavior. Log enough to diagnose the failed step while respecting private data and approval boundaries.

reading.section: Chapter 1: RAG and context; Chapter 2: ingestion and retrieval
reading.goal: Explain how a question becomes retrieved evidence and an answer.

reading.section: Chapter 2: tools, evaluation, security and resilience
reading.goal: Explain one tool boundary, one evaluation test and one recovery path.
Learn the basic model and data vocabulary before tackling a case study.
Compare evaluation methods and explain why a metric can miss useful meaning.

exercises.title: Design an in-memory cache
exercises.brief: Design a Python cache with get and put operations, a fixed capacity and least-recently-used eviction. Describe the contract before choosing a data structure. Start with one process and one thread.

steps.title: Clarify the contract
prompts: What happens when a key is missing?
Does updating a key change its position? What about zero capacity?

steps.title: Name the responsibilities
prompts: Which object owns values and eviction order?
What public interface will callers use?

steps.title: Describe state changes
prompts: Walk through put A, put B, get A, put C with capacity two.
Which invariants must hold after every operation?

steps.title: Sketch and test
prompts: Write the class outline and explain operation costs.
Choose tests for updates, missing keys and eviction.

followups: What changes if multiple threads call the cache?
How would expiry change the API and state?
review: I made the API behavior explicit.
I walked through an edge case and a trade-off.

exercises.title: Design a retryable task runner
exercises.brief: Design a small Python task runner that executes a job, reports status and retries temporary failures. Focus on object boundaries and testability; distributed deployment is a follow-up.

steps.title: Clarify behavior
prompts: Which failures should be retried?
What should a caller see after cancellation or permanent failure?

steps.title: Separate responsibilities
prompts: Who executes a job, chooses retry delays and stores status?
Which interfaces make a fake clock and fake task possible in tests?

steps.title: Model states
prompts: List valid transitions between pending, running, retrying and finished.
What stops a retry after cancellation?

steps.title: Sketch and test
prompts: Walk through failure followed by success.
Test retry limits and a job whose side effect is unsafe to repeat.

followups: What changes when jobs must survive a process crash?
How would two workers avoid doing the same job at once?
review: I separated execution from retry policy.
I described error and cancellation states.
I identified a side effect that needs duplicate protection.

exercises.title: Design a document-processing service
exercises.brief: Users upload documents and receive processing results later. Uploads arrive in bursts, workers can crash, and clients need job status. Choose explicit traffic and document-size assumptions for this exercise.

steps.title: Set requirements
prompts: What does a completed job produce?
Which matters most: upload latency, processing time, availability or cost?

steps.title: Define APIs and data
prompts: What are the upload, status and result APIs?
Where do files, job state and result references live?

steps.title: Draw the main flow
prompts: Trace one request from client to storage, queue and worker.
Explain why each service exists before adding more components.

steps.title: Stress the design
prompts: What happens after a worker crashes mid-job?
Where do you apply backpressure, retries and duplicate protection?

steps.title: Explain a trade-off
prompts: What breaks at ten times your assumed traffic?
Choose one bottleneck, one metric and one change.

followups: The same upload request is sent twice. What should the client observe?
One tenant sends most of the traffic. How do you protect other tenants?
review: I traced APIs and data ownership.
I explained failure recovery and one measurable bottleneck.

exercises.title: Design a notification service
exercises.brief: An application sends email and push notifications. Users choose preferences, providers can fail, and duplicate messages are undesirable. Define your scale and delivery expectations explicitly.

steps.title: Set requirements
prompts: Which notifications are urgent and which can wait?
What delivery and duplicate guarantees can you realistically promise?

steps.title: Define APIs and data
prompts: How are notification requests and user preferences represented?
How does a caller track delivery status?

steps.title: Draw the delivery path
prompts: Trace an event through routing, queues and provider adapters.
Where are ordering, rate limits and tenant boundaries enforced?

steps.title: Handle failures
prompts: A provider times out after sending a message. What do you do?
How do you handle permanent failures and a growing backlog?

steps.title: Explain a trade-off
prompts: What do you monitor for missed or delayed delivery?
Explain one cost versus reliability choice.

followups: How would you add a new provider without changing callers?
A user opts out while a message is queued. What should happen?
review: I stated a delivery guarantee and its limits.

exercises.title: Design an internal-document assistant
exercises.brief: Employees ask questions about internal documents. Answers should cite evidence, respect document permissions and admit when evidence is missing. Design the data and evaluation flow before selecting models.

steps.title: Define success
prompts: What makes an answer useful and what counts as a harmful failure?
What latency, freshness and cost assumptions will you use?

steps.title: Design retrieval
prompts: How are documents parsed, chunked and indexed?
Where do access checks happen, including during retrieval?

steps.title: Trace a question
prompts: Explain query processing, retrieval, answer generation and citations.
What happens if the retrieved evidence is weak or contradictory?

steps.title: Evaluate and recover
prompts: Build a small evaluation set with expected evidence and permission cases.
How do you separate retrieval failures from generation failures?

steps.title: Defend trade-offs
prompts: Why vectors, keyword search, a graph or a combination?
How will you update documents and monitor regressions?

followups: An employee loses document access. How quickly should cached answers change?
The model provider is unavailable. What can the assistant still do safely?
review: I designed abstention and evidence checks.
I described an evaluation set and failure-specific metrics.

exercises.title: Design a tool-using workflow assistant
exercises.brief: An assistant reads a request and proposes actions through tools. Some tools change data, calls can fail and the assistant has a limited budget. Define which actions need human approval in this exercise.

steps.title: Define the boundary
prompts: Which actions are allowed, and who approves consequential changes?
Which inputs and tool outputs should be treated as untrusted?

steps.title: Model the workflow
prompts: Separate reasoning, tool execution, authorization and durable state.
What state is needed to pause and resume safely?

steps.title: Trace execution
prompts: Walk through one request, including a tool failure.
How do you avoid repeating a completed write after losing its response?

steps.title: Evaluate behavior
prompts: Test tool selection, permission boundaries and unsupported requests.
What evidence shows the workflow helped rather than merely produced text?

steps.title: Control resources
prompts: Where are timeouts, retries and budgets enforced?
Explain what happens when the budget runs out or a provider fails.

followups: A tool response contains instructions to ignore the user. What happens?
How do you audit one failed workflow without exposing private data?
review: I separated model suggestions from authorized actions.
I explained duplicate protection and recovery.
I proposed behavioral evaluations and resource limits.
